Des femmes trans dénoncent le financemen: Trans women denounce provincial funding of feminist organization deemed transphobic
Les interventions de PDF Québec à l’Asse: PDF Québec’s interventions at the National Assembly don’t stop there.
Chaque année, le 8 mars marque la Journé: Every year, March 8 marks International Women’s Day. The day pays tribute to the rebels of the past, whose audacity made a more just world possible for women today. Many continue the fight, refusing to rest on the rights won by those who came before them. Claire Duclos, a recent law graduate of Université de Montréal’s Faculty of Law, is among these fighters.
Attablée devant un café pendant près de: Sitting over coffee for nearly two hours, Claire lists the inequalities she, like many trans women, runs into every day. She recounts how, from a very young age, she felt her body did not belong to her. In elementary school, the female roles in school plays became a refuge for her identity, then quickly a synonym for shame, brought on by the uncomprehending looks of her peers. Faced with these reactions, Claire locked herself into a pernicious cycle. To be a normal person, a “good person,” she had to suppress her unease, her pain, her self-disgust, and squeeze herself into the mould of biological sex.
Elle a suivi cette recette au pied de la: She followed that recipe to the letter until she arrived at university, at the expense of her mental health. Depression and suicidal thoughts surfaced. It was when she started university that she reconciled with her identity. “When I got to undergrad, I discovered new people and a welcoming community. By being confronted with other perspectives, I began to accept myself, to free myself from shame,” she explains, a hint of pride in her voice. While Claire feels welcomed by the LGBTQ+ community, she can’t say the same of certain feminist groups in Quebec. She believes the women of her community are not always welcome in those circles.
Pour les droits des femmes du Québec fai: Pour les droits des femmes du Québec is one of the feminist groups she points a finger at. “This kind of organization is nothing new, but what surprises me is that it’s being subsidized by the CAQ government,” she says with a deep sigh.
Comme son nom l’indique, Pour les droits: As its name suggests, Pour les droits des femmes du Québec (PDF Québec) aims to defend the rights of women in the province. A quick glance at its website is enough to conclude that it is a feminist group: it says its members fight to promote equality between women and men, bring women together across their differences, and combat hate propaganda and the violence women face. The organization has 500 to 600 members from all walks of life who advocate a universalist feminism.
Le groupe défend notamment la loi 21, ju: The group notably defends Bill 21, deemed “essential to achieving equality between women and men.” But let’s go back a little, to 2020 specifically, when the CAQ government wanted to table a bill to protect certain people from gender conversion therapy. As part of the study of this legislative initiative, PDF Québec submitted <l1>a brief</l1> to the National Assembly. In the document, its members suggest that these treatments could be considered non-affirming gender therapies that should not be penalized by the law. That is at least one reading that can be made of the list of recommendations found at the start of the organization’s brief.
Les interventions de PDF Québec à l’Asse: PDF Québec’s interventions at the National Assembly don’t stop there. One of its committees, the Groupe de réflexion sur l’identité de genre (GRIG), made itself heard during the drafting of <l1>Bill 2,</l1> which aimed to reform family law. In November 2021, the bill had provoked outrage in the trans community, notably because it required people to undergo sex reassignment surgery before changing the sex designation on official documents. The GRIG, however, argues that changing the sex designation should not be allowed at all, whether or not surgery has taken place. “It could encourage people to resort to it” [these operations], the committee writes in <l2>the brief</l2> it submitted to the government in December 2021.
Depuis 2019, PDF Québec reçoit un financ: Since 2019, PDF Québec has received annual funding from the Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Solidarity “in support of [its] overall mission.” The organization pocketed $119,553 in the 2019-2020 fiscal year. Diane Guilbault, PDF Québec’s president at the time, told Le Devoir in an interview that it was “financial assistance to help [its members] pursue [their] projects.” The funding was renewed in 2020 ($123,545), and the budget announced last March provides for $124,780 to be paid to the organization this year.
‍<strong>La fatigue de lutter pour être: ‍The exhaustion of fighting to be a woman
<strong>‍</strong>« Les actions de Pour: ‍“The actions of Pour les droits des femmes du Québec demonize trans people in the eyes of society,” says Céleste Trianon, a trans activist and spokesperson for the Centre de lutte contre l’oppression des genres. The activist believes the women of her community would not be welcome in the organization. Céleste Trianon says these women tend to hide their transphobic ideas behind a veil of feminist arguments. For example, PDF Québec members have signed several open letters published by La Presse and Le Devoir in which they portray trans people negatively. In the letter “Assimiler genre et sexe ? Tout le monde est concerné,” they warn young girls who decide to express their trans identity and denounce “the pressure on young people to buy into the theory that they could be ‘born in the wrong body.’” According to Céleste Trianon, who cites studies, this kind of discourse can harm trans people’s mental health by spreading disinformation and stereotypes about the community. “Growing up with gender dysphoria is already extremely alienating.
On peut se passer du jugement de la soci: We can do without society’s judgment, the insults and the daily violence that add to our mental load.” At age 17, Céleste Trianon took part in the lawsuit against the Attorney General of Quebec to make the legal procedures for changing name and sex easier for Quebecers. Bill 2, drafted by Simon Jolin-Barrette, was meant to respond to her demands, but “the government clearly didn’t understand the demands of trans people,” the spokesperson says indignantly. Today, she says she is exhausted from having to constantly defend her rights, which she does not have the luxury of taking for granted. “When the government introduced Bill 2, I had to get back to work to write <l1>a 47-page brief</l1> explaining that it was the most transphobic bill in the country’s history.” At that time, the activist devoted more than 30 hours a week to researching and writing the document, on top of being a student. “I’d like to be able to enjoy life and my rights the way cis people can, without constantly being on the defensive every time a new bill is announced,” the activist adds.
Le financement de PDF suscite un mélange: PDF’s funding provokes a mix of incomprehension and worry in Claire Duclos. “I don’t understand how a transphobic organization like PDF Québec can receive annual grants from a government that claims to listen to the trans community,” she says in an irritated tone. “Does that mean the CAQ condones PDF Québec’s positions?” the jurist asks.
« Je suis en colère, je suis furieuse, j: “I’m angry, I’m furious, I’m… every word that describes rage,” Céleste Trianon fumes. “I send money to the government, I pay my taxes, and I refuse to let my money end up in the pockets of an organization whose goal is to restrict my rights!” she adds. On behalf of their community, these women are making an impassioned plea: they demand that the government immediately stop using public funds to finance PDF Québec. Their voices are joined by that of Liberal MNA Jennifer Maccarone. Maccarone, who is the LGBTQ+ file spokesperson for the Liberal caucus, also finds this funding “unacceptable and unjustifiable.” “In the House, I asked the government to justify this funding, but I received no answer from it,” she says. In response to her concerns, the Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Solidarity maintains that “the organization’s mission is not being called into question.”
D’après celui-ci, PDF Québec remplit tou: According to the ministry, PDF Québec meets all the eligibility criteria of the Promotion of Rights component of the Programme de soutien financier aux orientations gouvernementales en action communautaire et en action bénévole. The ministry also spoke of “the government’s willingness to accept the open expression of diverse points of view from collective rights advocacy organizations, without this being perceived as undesirable and without interfering with financial support.” The Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Solidarity made no comment on PDF Québec’s positions.
<strong>‍</strong>« La semaine dernière: ‍“Just last week, the government supported a motion denouncing discrimination based on gender identity,” notes Québec solidaire (QS) co-spokesperson Manon Massé.
Dans cette motion déposée par son parti,: In the motion tabled by her party, the government committed to recognizing “the importance of funding trans community resources, which help protect the rights of gender-diverse communities.” According to the QS MNA, who is also in charge of LGBTQ+ issues in her party, “the government needs to finally walk the talk, and that has to be reflected in government funding.” She hopes “the government will act concretely to support them and fight all transphobic discourse.” Several organizations that defend the interests of trans people are currently underfunded, including TransEstrie, which could soon have to close its doors.
TransEstrie offre une panoplie de servic: TransEstrie offers a range of services to trans people living in the regions, where such community centres are rare. On the organization’s home page, the following message could be read: “Due to a lack of resources, we will close our services on April 1.” Thanks to a crowdfunding campaign and $20,000 in financial aid from Simon Jolin-Barrette’s ministry, the organization will be able to continue its activities beyond that date, to the great relief of the trans community. In all, $35,000 was raised.
Séré Beauchesne Lévesque, fondateur de T: Séré Beauchesne Lévesque, founder of TransEstrie, is delighted by this government aid, which will let the community centre survive a few more months. “We’ll be able to keep paying for our space, which also serves as a refuge for trans people in the Estrie looking for advice or even a roof over their heads,” the spokesperson explains. “This money will also let us pay for the treatments and name-change procedures of our less well-off clients.” For Séré Beauchesne Lévesque, PDF Québec’s funding is institutional transphobia: “For LGBTQ+ organizations, it’s very hard to get government funding because the existing programs don’t fit their activities and mission.”
« Si le gouvernement souhaite encourager: “If the government wants to support organizations that truly defend the rights of Quebec women, I can recommend plenty of organizations that serve the trans community and are desperately short of money,” suggests Céleste Trianon. “At least I’d have a clear conscience knowing my money is serving my community.”
PDF Québec n’avait toujours pas répondu: PDF Québec had still not responded to our interview requests at the time of publication.
